slides.notes: My name is [Insert Student Name], and this is my final-semester review of the Page Summarizer project. Version 1 sent the page text to a cloud service. Version 2 runs a small language model inside Chrome, on this laptop. I will explain the AI parts in plain words, then show what was built and what was measured.

slides.notes: I will go through six parts. First, Version 1 and what it could not do. Then I explain what a language model is, how it writes, and how the model gets onto the laptop. Next are the parts that run it, the popup, the errors and the setup. After that come the tests, the measured results and the problems I met. I finish with what is not done yet, the demo plan and questions.

slides.title: Version 1 and its limits
bullets: Version 1 summarizes the open page with a free Gemini key, pasted once into the popup.
Each part of a page is sent to Google, so the page text leaves this laptop.
Every summary needs the internet, and the free quota ran out during the live runs.
Version 2 keeps the popup, the page reader and the job handling. Only the engine changes.
slides.notes: Version 1 has one promise. A reader presses one button on an open page and gets a short summary in the popup. The reader pastes a free key once, and each part of the page is then sent to Google. So the page text leaves this laptop, and every summary needs the internet. Version 2 keeps the same popup, page reader and job handling, and only the engine changes.

slides.title: What Version 2 changes
rows: Llama 3.2 1B on this laptop's graphics (SmolLM2 360M as a Fast choice)
Needed: a free key, pasted in the popup
Quota named by the service (15 a minute for the default model)
No service quota; a page over 12 parts is refused
A long page in about 2 minutes on built-in Intel graphics (124.6 s measured); a short page in 15 to 18 s on NVIDIA
slides.caption: Summary quality was not measured in either version. Version 1 timings are in the mid-semester deck.
slides.notes: This table sets Version 2 next to Version 1. The model now lives on the laptop, so there is no key and no cloud. The page text stays on the laptop, and the only internet use is the one-time download of about 695 megabytes. Speed depends on the graphics chip. The client's laptop has only built-in Intel graphics, so I measured that case: a long Wikipedia page takes about two minutes. I did not measure summary quality in either version with a score, so I only say what I saw in the saved summaries.

slides.title: What a language model is, and the numbers
left: A language model guesses the next piece of text, one piece at a time.
Learning set its stored numbers, called parameters. The project only reads them.
The model here is Llama 3.2 1B, tuned to follow plain requests in English.
right: A token is a piece of text, about four characters of English. A rule of thumb.
A part of 6,000 characters is about 1,500 tokens.
Context window: 4,096 tokens. Like a desk that holds only so many pages.
The instructions, the part and the answer must all fit in it at once.
slides.notes: A language model is a program that guesses the next piece of text. Learning set its stored numbers, which are called parameters, and this project only reads them. The model reads and writes tokens, and a token is about four characters of English. Its context window is the text it can hold in one request, which is 4,096 tokens for this model. So the project cuts a long page into parts of about 1,500 tokens.

slides.title: How a model writes: reading, then one token at a time
rows: Reads the whole prompt in one pass, like scanning a page first
One new token per step, and each step looks back at everything before it
34 to 53 tokens a second in clean runs; about 63 in the speed test
The graphics programs are compiled once, like warming up an oven
About 30 s on first use; 0.5 s in a later offline run
Stops at the last token, or at 300 tokens a part (320 for the final summary)
Set in the configuration file; not a measurement
slides.caption: The 34 to 53 range is from saved clean runs. The run after the label fix reached 65 and 45 (slide 20). The speed test has no saved run file.
slides.notes: The model works in two stages. First it reads the whole prompt in one pass, which the report calls prefill. Then it writes the answer one token at a time, which is called decode, and that stage is the slow one. The saved clean runs wrote 34 to 53 tokens a second on this laptop. A separate speed test measured about 63, and it has no saved run file, so I label it as a test.

slides.title: Getting the model onto the laptop
left: Most stored numbers are kept in 4 bits, not 16. The model name q4f16_1 says so.
One billion numbers at 4 bits take about 0.5 GB, so some parts keep more bits.
The cost is precision. The answers can differ a little from the full model.
right: WebGPU lets Chrome send the work to the graphics card.
The card must support 16-bit math (shader-f16). Without it the popup refuses to run.
On first use the graphics programs are compiled: about 30 s of warm-up.
slides.notes: Two ideas make the model small enough to run here. The first is 4-bit compression. Most stored numbers are rounded to 4 bits, which brings the file down to about 695 MB. The second is WebGPU, the browser's way to run work on the graphics card. The first use also waits about half a minute while the card compiles its programs.

slides.title: The layers, and what each one does
rows: Owns the job, the parts and the merge
Keeps the model loaded; closes after 5 minutes idle
Runs WebLLM's handler, so the page stays responsive
Reads the model, splits text into tokens, runs each answer
Does the calculations on the graphics card
slides.caption: The popup only shows progress. Closing it does not stop the job.
slides.notes: The extension has layers. The popup only has a button and shows progress. The service worker owns the job, and it asks a hidden offscreen page to do the heavy work. That page holds the loaded model and runs a web worker, which runs the WebLLM library. WebLLM sends the calculations to the graphics card through WebGPU.

slides.title: Where the model files live, and the offline proof
rows: Kept between runs; no code deletes them
Offscreen page writes on first use
Until the browser closes; removed when its tab closes
Until the page closes, 5 minutes after the last message
slides.caption: Offline proof: with the outside websites blocked, the short article took 17.7 s after the label fix (15.3 s before it). No API key is stored.
slides.notes: The model files are kept in IndexedDB, which is the browser's own storage for the extension. The job record sits in session storage, and it is removed when its tab closes. The loaded model lives in graphics memory and is freed after five idle minutes. For the offline proof, I blocked the outside websites and ran the short article, which took 17.7 seconds after the label fix.

slides.title: The hidden offscreen page and its messages
rows: Asks for the graphics card, whether the model is stored, and its size
Loads the model into the graphics card
Sends the phase, the percentage and the text, many times
Asks for one summary; the reply has the text and the stats
Sent every 10 s while work runs, so the worker stays awake
slides.caption: The page has no tabs and no chrome.storage access, so it works by messages only. It closes 5 minutes after its last running message ends.
slides.notes: The offscreen page is a hidden page that Chrome lets an extension open for a heavy task. It has no tabs and no storage access, so it talks only by messages. The service worker sends three kinds of request, and the page sends progress and keepalive messages back. The page closes five minutes after its last message ends, and that frees the graphics memory.

slides.title: Graphics card check and choice of model
header: What the extension does, and what the reader sees
rows: Refuses before any job. A red line explains why, and the button is disabled.
Keeps the main model, shows a note that answers can be slow, and reads at most 6,000 characters of a long page.
Uses SmolLM2 360M: about 2 times quicker, but summaries are often muddled or wrong.
Picks SmolLM2 360M. The rule has not been seen on real low-memory hardware.
Main model runs out of graphics memory
Tries SmolLM2 360M once. The summary carries a notice that it may be less detailed, and the choice is kept.
slides.caption: The extension makes these choices, except Quality, which the reader sets. The main model is about 695 MB; SmolLM2 360M is about 204 MB.
slides.notes: The extension checks the graphics card before anything else. Without WebGPU or the 16-bit math feature it refuses and says why. On built-in graphics, like the client's laptop, it keeps the accurate main model and instead reads less of a long page. The reader can choose Fast in Settings, which uses the small model, but I measured that its summaries are often wrong. A memory failure also sends the extension to the small model, and that choice stays until the stored settings are cleared.

slides.title: Built-in graphics: reading is the slow part
left: Llama 3.2 1B: reads 15.6 and writes 2 tokens a second.
Reading is about 80% of the time of one part.
The client's laptop has this kind of chip (Iris Xe).
right: Llama 3.2 1B: writes 34 to 53 tokens a second in clean runs.
Reads about 600 tokens a second (speed test, not a saved run).
Short article, model stored: 15.3 s before the label fix, 17.7 s after.
The developer laptop has both chips; the client's has only the Intel one.
slides.notes: I measured how fast each small model reads and writes on the built-in Intel chip. Reading is the slow part: the chip reads only 15 to 40 tokens a second, whatever the model size, and a normal part of 6,000 characters is about 1,440 tokens. That is why one part takes a minute or more, and why a smaller model does not help much. The separate NVIDIA card reads about 40 times faster. The developer laptop has both chips, but the client's laptop has only the Intel one, so the Intel numbers are the ones that matter for the client. All of these numbers are from a hidden test browser on the developer laptop, not from the client's laptop.

slides.title: Long pages: read less on slow chips
header: Wikipedia Lighthouse page, built-in Intel graphics
rows: Text the extension reads from the page
After cutting Notes, Bibliography and [12] markers
Now: Llama 3.2 1B, opening plus first sentences, 1 part
Popup's guess for reading the whole page
Same page on NVIDIA, whole page, 7 parts
slides.caption: Built-in graphics read a part of 6,000 characters in about a minute, so the extension reads less. A button reads the whole page.
slides.notes: A long page costs time in proportion to the text the model must read. On the Wikipedia Lighthouse page, a quarter of the text is notes and bibliography, so that is cut first. On built-in graphics the extension then keeps the opening in full and the first sentences of the paragraphs, spread over the page, which is about 6,000 characters or one part. The popup says how much was read, and a button reads the whole page if the person wants it. This took the Lighthouse page from 616 seconds to 125 seconds, and the summary was accurate. The cost is coverage: the summary rests on about a fifth of the text.

slides.title: Errors and fallbacks: the main messages
rows: Chrome cannot use your graphics card for the model (WebGPU is not available). Open chrome://gpu to check.
Your graphics card does not support the 16-bit math this model needs, so this computer cannot run Version 2.
The graphics card ran out of memory. Close other heavy tabs or programs and try again.
The model download stopped. Check your internet connection and press the button again. What was already downloaded is kept.
This page is too long for the local model on this computer. Try a shorter page.
The model took too long to answer. Try again, or use a shorter page.
slides.caption: 13 codes in all; six are shown. Also: TOO_LITTLE_TEXT, RESTRICTED_PAGE, INTERRUPTED, MODEL_LOAD_FAILED, EMPTY_ANSWER, EXTRACT_FAILED, SERVICE_ERROR.
slides.notes: Every failure has one code and one plain message. The reader sees the message in the popup, and the technical detail goes to the console. The table shows six of the thirteen codes. Two of the refusals happen before any download: a page that is too long, and a page that Chrome does not let an extension read.

slides.title: Setup for the client: four scripts and one manual step
rows: Checks Chrome 116 or newer and the extension files. Ends with SETUP COMPLETE or SETUP FAILED.
Opens Chrome's extensions page and shows the four steps. The folder path is on the clipboard.
Prints the Windows version, memory, graphics chips and free space on drive C.
Opt-in only. Writes one per-user Windows value so Chrome uses the separate card. Undo: set-chrome-gpu.ps1 -Remove.
Only on two-chip laptops. Nothing to do on the client's laptop.
slides.caption: Chrome 137 and later cannot load an extension from a flag. The user clicks Load unpacked and selects the folder.
slides.notes: The client uses four scripts. setup.bat checks Chrome and the files, and it ends with SETUP COMPLETE or SETUP FAILED. run.bat opens the extensions page, and the client clicks Load unpacked by hand. check-computer.ps1 reports the laptop's memory, graphics chips and free space. The setup.bat --gpu option changes a Windows setting, so it runs only when the client asks for it. The client's laptop has one graphics chip, so the graphics switch is not needed there. The first use downloads about 695 megabytes.

slides.title: How it was tested

stats.label: unit tests, with no browser and no network
Windows script checks, B1 to B10c

slides.caption: Most browser tests use a pretend model, so failures such as no WebGPU can be forced on purpose. The real model was run separately.
slides.notes: The tests run at three levels. There are 93 unit tests, which check the small rules without a browser or a network. There are 31 browser scenarios, which run in a hidden Chromium with a pretend model, and they all pass. The 15 Windows script checks test the batch files and the PowerShell scripts. The four clean real-model run files are the only numbers I quote for speed.

slides.title: Problems met and how they were fixed
rows: Chrome used the weak Intel chip: about 2 tokens a second, a 36 s first answer
A warm-up step and an on-screen note on Intel. The speed work in the last row later replaced the automatic smaller model.
WebLLM's model cache failed inside the offscreen page (CacheStorage error)
Switched WebLLM to IndexedDB and asked for unlimitedStorage, so the browser keeps the model files.
The small model wrote summaries with nothing on screen to say so
A notice now sits above a summary written by the smaller model. The model line refreshes when a job ends.
A stored model was labeled Downloading for about 0.8 s
The offscreen page checks the store first, so a stored model always shows as loading. Unit test added.
Real Chrome, long Wikipedia page, Intel chip: a vague error with no reason
A part too long for the model is cut in half and retried. The answer limit is 10 minutes. The popup now shows a technical detail line.
Ten minutes for a long page on built-in graphics (the client's chip)
Measured: reading is the cost. Read less of a long page, keep the accurate model: 616 s down to 125 s.
slides.caption: Found and fixed on 21, 24 and 26 October 2026. Each one is written in the development log.
slides.notes: I met four real problems on 21 October, and each one is written in the development log. The first was the graphics chip: Chrome picked the weak Intel chip, so the first answers were very slow. The second was the model cache, which failed inside the hidden page until I switched the storage. The third was silent: the small model wrote summaries with no sign on screen. The fourth was a wrong Downloading line on a model that was already stored. The fifth problem came from the real Chrome on 24 October. On the long Wikipedia page the popup only said that something went wrong inside the extension. I repeated it in a hidden browser and found two weak spots: one answer on the Intel chip took longer than the three-minute limit, and a part that did not fit the model's window was reported as a vague error. Now such a part is cut in half and tried again, the answer limit is ten minutes, and the popup shows a technical detail line. The sixth problem came from the client's laptop details. It has only built-in graphics, and a long page took about ten minutes there. I measured where the time went and found it was reading, not writing. I asked a stronger model for advice, and then built the shorter reading. The Lighthouse page went from 616 seconds to 125 seconds.

slides.title: What is not done or not verified
bullets: Client's laptop: details known (Iris Xe, 16 GB, Chrome 156), but never run there.
Speed numbers are from a hidden browser on the developer laptop; a visible window may differ.
setup.bat --gpu: tested only on a test registry key; not needed on the client's laptop.
A shortened summary covers about a fifth of a long page; the whole page takes 5 to 12 minutes.
English only. Small-model slips. Another engine (Transformers.js) was not tried.
Cutting a long part in half is tested with the pretend model only.
slides.notes: Some things are not finished, and I want to be exact about them. The client's laptop details are known, but I have not run the extension on it, so its real speed is not measured. All my speed numbers come from a hidden test browser on the developer laptop, and a visible window might be faster or slower. A shortened summary rests on about a fifth of a long page, and reading the whole page takes five to twelve minutes on this kind of chip. The model is small and made for English. I did not try a different engine, because a stronger model advised me to measure in a visible window first. Cutting a too-long part in half is covered by unit tests and the pretend model, because no real part overflowed the window.

slides.title: Demo plan: what I will show, in order
bullets: Show the card loaded from chrome://extensions. There is no key and no cloud box.
Open the Lighthouse article, summarize: about 2 minutes on built-in graphics (124.6 s measured), with the shortened-page notice.
Close the popup, wait five seconds, and reopen it. The job is still there.
Turn off Wi-Fi and summarize a short article. Say which run: 17.7 s after the label fix, 15.3 s before it.
Open chrome://version and a near-empty page to show the two refusals.
Do not show the first download live: it takes minutes. Do not press Read the whole page in front of an audience.
slides.notes: The demo follows the steps in the knowledge-transfer document. I start from the extensions page, so the audience sees that no key is needed. Then I summarize the Lighthouse article, and after that I turn off the network for a short article. I also show two refusals, so the audience sees that the code stops early.
